title: Global Enviro Inc. & Ian George McIntyre (AB Courts)
subject: Alberta criminal prosecution of Global Enviro Inc. and Ian George McIntyre for fraudulent SR&ED tax claims.
outcome: Corporation and director convicted under s. 239(1.1) for wilfully claiming an unentitled ITC; $250,000 fine each, upheld on appeal.
summary: In R. v. Global Enviro Inc. and Ian George McIntyre, Alberta courts convicted a Calgary corporation and its director of wilfully claiming an unentitled SR&ED investment tax credit under subsection 239(1.1) of the Income Tax Act. Each received a $250,000 fine, showing that misleading CRA auditors about when work was performed exposes directors to personal penal liability.
metaDescription: Explore the Alberta Court of Queen's Bench and Provincial Court decisions in Global Enviro Inc. and Ian George McIntyre.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural Posture and Judicial Identification

The decisions of the Provincial Court of Alberta and the Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta in R. v. Global Enviro Inc. and Ian George McIntyre represent a watershed moment in the enforcement of the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program under the federal Income Tax Act (Canada), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA"). Unlike the vast majority of Canadian SR&ED disputes—which are adjudicated as civil appeals of Notices of Reassessment before the Tax Court of Canada—this proceeding was prosecuted in the criminal and penal courts of Alberta as a summary conviction offence for tax fraud and false statements under subsection 239(1.1) of the ITA.

The litigation unfolded across two judicial levels in Calgary, Alberta. At first instance, the matter was heard in the Provincial Court of Alberta under Docket 060808508P10101-0102, resulting in the trial judgment cited as R. v. Global Enviro Inc., 2009 ABPC 76, delivered on March 17, 2009. The original Information charged three defendants jointly: the corporate claimant, Global Enviro Inc. ("GEI"); its director, Ian George McIntyre; and a third individual co-defendant, Patrick Glen Page. Following conviction and sentencing on the second count of the Information at the Provincial Court level, Global Enviro Inc. and Ian George McIntyre appealed both their convictions and sentences to the Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta, sitting as a summary conviction appeal court pursuant to Part XXVII of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46. In the appellate ruling rendered on January 20, 2011, under Docket 060808508 S2 and cited as R. v. Global Enviro Inc., 2011 ABQB 32, the Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta dismissed the appeals and affirmed the trial dispositions in their entirety.
Factual Matrix and the Taxpayer's SR&ED Claim

Global Enviro Inc. was a Calgary-based corporation whose SR&ED claim, identified on Form T661 as project "#02A EX-CEL BITUMEN SEPARATION SYSTEM," concerned a prototype system that used a surfactant and a washing vessel to separate oil (bitumen and other hydrocarbons) from sands and clays; the claim did not concern waste gasification units. As detailed in the Agreed Statement of Facts entered at trial as Exhibit 84, which outlined the corporate structure of Global Enviro Inc., Ian George McIntyre served as a director and controlling mind of the corporation along with Robert Bateman, while Patrick Glen Page was a director and controlling mind of a separate corporation, Ex-Cel Environmental Inc.

On or about January 7, 2003, Global Enviro Inc. filed its first T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (dated November 21, 2002 and signed by its Vice President, Robert Bateman) for the taxation year June 1, 2001 to May 31, 2002, together with Schedule 31 and Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) Form T661 E(01), Claim for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) in Canada, which was dated January 6, 2003, received by the CRA on or about January 8, 2003, and certified by J. R. Bateman. Through this filing, Global Enviro Inc. reported qualified current SR&ED expenditures of $923,437, consisting entirely of contract expenditures, and claimed an SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) of $323,202.95, being 35% of the expenses claimed; the subsequent fine of $250,000 imposed on each appellant represented approximately 77% of that amount.

The core factual defect underlying the claim was that the work on which it was based had largely been performed before the claim period, while the supporting invoices—from Ex-Cel Environmental Inc. ($780,887), Ian McIntyre ($100,800) and WHMIS Inc. ($41,750), each dated May 31, 2002—were prepared within it. Specifically, the claim filed in January 2003 asserted that the bitumen separation prototype was developed within the taxation year June 1, 2001 to May 31, 2002 when, in reality, much of the work had been done earlier: the photographs filed with the claim were date-stamped 1998, the year the prototype was built, and Mr. Page testified that the product had been developed over the previous five years. Based on the evidentiary record established at trial, the CRA auditors made clear that the expenditures, construction and testing of the bitumen separation system all had to have occurred during the claimed taxation year of June 1, 2001 to May 31, 2002; neither court ruled on which work, if any, qualified as SR&ED, the appellate court noting that it was not the Tax Court. The claim was not driven by a missed filing deadline; rather, the claim's preparer, Rick Velhat, had told the appellants that work done before the claim period could be claimed as long as the invoices were dated within it, and the trial judge accepted that, at the time of filing, Mr. McIntyre and Global honestly believed the claim was valid.
The Crown's Challenge and Governing Statutory Framework

Rather than restricting its enforcement action to a civil audit disallowance and administrative gross negligence penalties under subsection 163(2) of the ITA, the matter proceeded as a prosecution under section 239 of the ITA, with the Public Prosecution Service of Canada appearing for the Crown on the appeal. The Crown laid two specific charges under subsection 239(1.1) of the ITA, which governs offences specifically relating to tax refunds and credits. Under Count 1, the Crown alleged that on or about January 7, 2003, at or near Calgary, Alberta, the defendants Global Enviro Inc., Ian George McIntyre, and Patrick Glen Page claimed a refund or credit under the Income Tax Act of Canada to which they or any other person was not entitled by making, participating in, assenting to or acquiescing in the making of false or deceptive statements in the T2 Return of Income of Global Enviro Inc. and in its SR&ED claim for the period from June 1, 2001 to May 31, 2002, contrary to paragraph 239(1.1)(a) of the ITA. Under Count 2, the Crown alleged that between May 31, 2001 and July 24, 2003, both dates inclusive, at or near Calgary, Alberta, the defendants wilfully in any manner claimed an Investment Tax Credit under the Income Tax Act of Canada to which they or any other person was not entitled, contrary to paragraph 239(1.1)(e) of the ITA.

To adjudicate these penal charges, the Alberta courts operated within the intersecting statutory architecture of the federal SR&ED regime and the penal enforcement provisions of the ITA. At the substantive foundation of the program, subsection 248(1) of the ITA defines "scientific research and experimental development" as systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, encompassing basic research, applied research, and experimental development undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement, alongside prescribed support work commensurate with the needs and directly in support of such investigation.

The expenditure pooling and temporal filing mechanics are governed by section 37 of the ITA, wherein subsection 37(1) permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct current SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada directly by the taxpayer or "on behalf of the taxpayer". Crucially, subsection 37(11) combined with subsection 37(12) mandates that a taxpayer must file the prescribed form (Form T661) containing prescribed information in respect of an expenditure on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred, establishing an absolute 18-month post-fiscal-year-end statutory bar for corporations. If a taxpayer fails to file Form T661 within this strict statutory window, the expenditure is permanently deemed never to have been an expenditure on SR&ED. Concurrently, subsection 127(9) defines a "qualified expenditure" for Investment Tax Credit purposes, while section 127.1 enables Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) to claim a refundable Investment Tax Credit via Schedule T2SCH31.

When a claimant crosses the threshold from civil non-compliance into deliberate misrepresentation, subsection 239(1.1) of the ITA enacts specific criminal prohibitions targeting false or deceptive statements made to obtain tax credits or refunds. Under paragraphs 239(1.1)(g) and (h), every person who commits an offence under subsection 239(1.1) is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction and, in addition to any penalty otherwise provided in the ITA, is liable to a mandatory fine of not less than 50% and not more than 200% of the amount by which the refund or credit claimed exceeded the amount to which the person was entitled, or to both that fine and imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years. Furthermore, section 242 of the ITA pierces the corporate veil in penal proceedings by imposing personal liability on corporate directors, officers, or agents who directed, authorized, assented to, acquiesced in, or participated in the commission of the offence.
Final Holdings of the Provincial Court and Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta

In the trial judgment (2009 ABPC 76), Judge J.D. Bascom of the Provincial Court of Alberta carefully parsed the evidentiary record, including the Agreed Statement of Facts (Exhibit 84), the testimony of CRA auditors Dr. Chandra Patel and Ms. Velma Quonn, and the viva voce testimony of Mr. McIntyre, Mr. Page and the claim preparer Rick Velhat regarding the preparation of the SR&ED claim. The trial judge acquitted the appellants on Count 1 because he accepted that, when the claim was filed, Mr. McIntyre honestly believed—based on Mr. Velhat's advice—that work performed before the claim period could be claimed, but convicted both Global Enviro Inc. and its director Ian George McIntyre on Count 2, finding that after the March 24, 2003 audit meeting in Medicine Hat, at which the CRA auditors made clear that the work had to be performed between June 1, 2001 and May 31, 2002, Mr. McIntyre attempted to mislead the CRA (by attributing the 1998 date stamps on the photographs to an incorrectly set camera and by providing the WHMIS invoice, his own May 31, 2002 invoice and an intentionally vague letter faxed on April 3, 2003), and that the appellants thereby wilfully claimed an investment tax credit to which they were not entitled between May 31, 2001 and July 24, 2003; Patrick Glen Page was acquitted on both counts.

At sentencing, the statutory range under paragraph 239(1.1)(g) of the ITA required a fine of not less than 50% and not more than 200% of the amount by which the credit claimed exceeded the credit to which the claimant was entitled, with up to two years' incarceration also available under paragraph 239(1.1)(h). The Provincial Court sentenced Global Enviro Inc. to a fine of $250,000.00 and sentenced Ian George McIntyre personally to an additional fine of $250,000.00—each fine equating to approximately 77% of the $323,202.95 SR&ED credit claimed, a level the Court of Queen's Bench later described as being on the low end of the statutory range.

On appeal (2011 ABQB 32), heard on December 2, 2010 before Madam Justice B.L. Rawlins, the appellants challenged both the convictions and the sentences, arguing in substance that they should not be convicted if they genuinely believed Global was entitled to the credit, that the Crown had to prove Global was not entitled to any SR&ED credit at all, and that the sentences were excessive; the Court assessed the conviction appeals under the grounds in paragraph 686(1)(a) of the Criminal Code—an unreasonable verdict, a wrong decision on a question of law, or a miscarriage of justice. Applying the appellate standard of review articulated by the Supreme Court of Canada in R. v. W.(R.), [1992] 2 S.C.R. 122, which calls for great deference to a trial judge's findings of credibility (Justice Beck's directions in R. v. Covert, referenced at paragraph 12, were applied by the trial judge to assess Mr. McIntyre's testimony, not by the appellate court), the Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta held that the convictions rested on findings of fact rather than on a question of law, that the trial judge's findings that Mr. McIntyre understood the CRA's position after the March 24, 2003 meeting and then provided misleading information were not unreasonable, and that the appellants had in any event conceded that Global was not entitled to the credit. The appellate court concluded that, on the totality of the evidence, a properly instructed trier of fact could reasonably have reached the conclusion that the appellants had wilfully claimed SR&ED tax credits to which they were not entitled beyond a reasonable doubt. Both the conviction appeals and sentence appeals were consequently dismissed.
Core Legal, Technical, and Evidentiary Failures

A rigorous legal examination—combining the explicit judicial findings in 2009 ABPC 76 and 2011 ABQB 32 with the statutory mechanics of sections 37, 127, 239(1.1), and 248(1) of the ITA and related Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence cited alongside Global Enviro—reveals four fatal legal, technical, contractual, and evidentiary failures which, combined with the appellants' misleading conduct after the March 24, 2003 CRA audit meeting, transformed a disallowed SR&ED claim into a criminal conviction.
Temporal Cut-Off Violations and Retroactive Expenditure Shifting

The primary legal and factual catalyst for the prosecution in Global Enviro was the mismatch between the claimed taxation year (June 1, 2001 to May 31, 2002) and the period in which the work had actually been performed, compounded after the March 24, 2003 audit meeting by Mr. McIntyre's misleading explanations and documents about when the work was done. In Canadian tax law, the SR&ED regime operates on a strict fiscal-period cut-off basis governed by subsections 37(1), 37(11), and 127(9) of the ITA. For an expenditure to qualify for an ITC in a given taxation year, the underlying SR&ED work must be performed, and the expenditure must be legally incurred, within that specific fiscal period (subject to the 180-day unpaid amount rule in subsection 127(26)). Furthermore, under subsection 37(11), the prescribed Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 must be filed within 18 months of the end of the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred.

In Global Enviro, the evidentiary record established that much of the work underlying the claim had been performed before June 1, 2001—the prototype had been built in 1998, and Mr. McIntyre's own invoice covered December 1, 2000 to May 31, 2002—whereas the CRA required the work to have been performed during the claimed taxation year of June 1, 2001 to May 31, 2002. However, when filing in January 2003, Global Enviro Inc. submitted Form T661 for the June 1, 2001 to May 31, 2002 taxation year supported by invoices dated May 31, 2002 that covered work performed before that period, on its claim preparer's advice that such work could be claimed if invoiced within the claim period. In Canadian corporate tax practice, claimants frequently fall into this temporal trap through two recurring mechanisms. First, when the 18-month statutory filing deadline under subsection 37(11) for an earlier fiscal year expires, or when a prior taxation year was filed without an SR&ED claim, management may attempt to improperly roll forward historical R&D costs and technical narratives into a subsequent open taxation year. Second, where pre-incorporation or predecessor-entity technical development occurred prior to the claimant's active fiscal period, management may attempt to backstop or re-date contractor invoices and engineering milestones into the claimant's current taxation year. Although the trial judge found that the appellants honestly believed the claim was valid when Form T661 was filed, and therefore acquitted them of the paragraph 239(1.1)(a) charge, the claim disregarded the principle of annual tax accounting under section 9 and section 37 of the ITA, and the appellants' subsequent attempts to mislead the CRA auditors about when the work was performed grounded their conviction for wilfully claiming an unentitled credit under paragraph 239(1.1)(e).
Corporate Structure, Subcontractor Attribution, and Work Performed on Behalf of the Claimant

A second critical failure, illustrated by the Agreed Statement of Facts (Exhibit 84)—which outlined the corporate structure of Global Enviro Inc. and showed that its $923,437 claim consisted of contract expenditures, including $780,887 invoiced by Ex-Cel Environmental Inc. (controlled by co-accused Patrick Page), $100,800 invoiced by director Ian McIntyre himself, and $41,750 invoiced by WHMIS Inc.—involves the statutory nexus between the corporate claimant, related entities, and third-party performers. Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i) and (i.01) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, a taxpayer may only claim SR&ED expenditures for work carried on in Canada directly by the taxpayer or "on behalf of the taxpayer".

Where multiple corporate entities, predecessors, joint ventures, or outside engineering contractors are involved in developing environmental technology such as GEI's bitumen separation system, Canadian tax law imposes strict legal and contractual prerequisites. First, privity and technical direction must exist at the exact time of performance: for work performed by a contractor or related entity to constitute SR&ED performed "on behalf of" the claimant, a binding contractual arrangement must be in place while the work is executed under which the performer undertakes the systematic investigation for the claimant's benefit and under the claimant's technical direction and financial risk. Second, the ITA strictly prohibits retroactive inter-company reallocation: a newly formed or restructured corporation cannot retroactively adopt or claim SR&ED expenditures originally incurred by a separate legal entity, promoter, or sister company in an earlier period by issuing ex post facto management fees or backdated inter-company invoices. Third, transactions between non-arm's length parties are subject to strict cost-look-through rules and transfer-pricing caps under subsections 37(13) and 127(11.6) to (11.8) of the ITA, while arm's length contract payments are restricted to 80% inclusion for ITC purposes and must exclude commercial capital asset acquisitions or turnkey equipment fabrication. In Global Enviro, the courts did not rule on attribution as such, but the record showed that work performed in earlier years by Mr. Page and Ex-Cel was invoiced to Global within the claim period on the preparer's advice that this was acceptable because Global was acquiring the technology, that the CRA auditor questioned whether the relationship was non-arm's length, and that Mr. McIntyre's invoice described coordinating research and development when, during the claim period, he was in fact raising money for Global.
Substantive SR&ED Eligibility Deficiencies and Form T661 Misrepresentations

In Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, the boundary between civil technical disagreement and penal fraud is evaluated against the substantive five-question eligibility framework established by the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 1998 CanLII 568 (TCC), and applied in subsequent cases such as Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen, 2006 TCC 597. Under the Northwest Hydraulic standard, a claimant must establish five cumulative elements: first, whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; second, whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty; third, whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses; fourth, whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; and fifth, whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed.

Canadian legal commentary analyzing Global Enviro alongside Northwest Hydraulic and Zeuter Development emphasizes a decisive spectrum of taxpayer conduct across these criteria. In Northwest Hydraulic (1998), the claimant contested five hydraulic engineering projects disallowed by the CRA; the taxpayer succeeded on four projects where genuine technological uncertainties and advancements were proven, and lost only the fifth project on a civil basis because the scope and possibility of technological advancement had been overstated. In Zeuter Development (2006), the claimant developed an online learning tool for high school students and claimed SR&ED from 1995 to 2002. Although the CRA approved credits up to 1999, it rejected all claims from 2000 onward because the foundational technological uncertainties had already been resolved and subsequent work constituted routine software development. Because the claimant in Zeuter suffered from genuine confusion regarding ongoing eligibility after receiving prior audit approvals, no penal sanctions were imposed, though all post-1999 credits were denied.

By stark contrast, in Global Enviro (2009/2011)—and subsequently in R. v. Les éléments chauffants Tempora inc., 2017 QCCQ 2684, and R. v. Avard, 2014 QCCQ 9716—the criminal liability did not turn on whether the bitumen separation work satisfied subsection 248(1); the appellate court expressly declined to determine the validity of the SR&ED claim, stating that it was not the Tax Court. Rather, after learning at the March 24, 2003 audit meeting that the work had to have been performed between June 1, 2001 and May 31, 2002, Mr. McIntyre and Global provided false and misleading explanations and documentation—an invoice describing R&D coordination when he had in fact been fundraising, a WHMIS invoice for work not performed in January to May 2002, and an intentionally vague letter—in an attempt to show that the claimed work occurred within the claimed taxation period.
Evidentiary Deficiencies, Mens Rea, and the Transition from Civil Disallowance to Penal Liability

In a standard civil appeal before the Tax Court of Canada, the taxpayer bears the initial burden of demolishing the Minister's factual assumptions on a balance of probabilities, and a lack of contemporaneous documentation—required under the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic and subsection 230(1) of the ITA—simply results in the civil denial of the ITC claim. In Global Enviro, however, the proceeding was a criminal prosecution under subsection 239(1.1) of the ITA, where the Crown bore the burden of proving both the actus reus and the subjective mens rea (wilfulness) beyond a reasonable doubt.

The evidentiary record before the Provincial Court of Alberta and the Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta demonstrated how documentary contradictions and affirmative misstatements establish criminal mens rea. First, a direct contradiction existed between the evidence and the filed Form T661: Form T661 E(01) was signed by officer J. R. Bateman under a certification that the form and related schedules were true, correct, and complete, yet the evidence—including photographs date-stamped 1998, Mr. Page's acknowledgement to the auditors that some of the work had been done earlier, and Mr. McIntyre's own notes—showed that the claimed work had largely been performed before the June 1, 2001 to May 31, 2002 claim period. Second, the trial judge accepted the defence of reliance on Mr. Velhat's advice up to the filing date (hence the acquittal on Count 1), but rejected as not credible Mr. McIntyre's claimed inability to recall the March 24, 2003 audit meeting and inferred wilfulness from his subsequent misleading statements and documents. On appeal in 2011 ABQB 32, the appellants argued that they could not be convicted if they genuinely believed Global was entitled to the credit, irrespective of the CRA's position, an argument the Court held miscast what the Crown was required to prove. In Canadian tax evasion jurisprudence, mens rea under section 239 encompasses intentional fraud as well as recklessness or wilful blindness—where a corporate director knows that substantive work was completed in an earlier fiscal period or by a different entity, yet signs or acquiesces in a Form T661 claiming those amounts in a subsequent period without an honest belief in their validity. The Court of Queen's Bench, deferring to the trial judge's credibility findings, held that the finding that Global Enviro Inc. and McIntyre wilfully claimed a credit to which they were not entitled was neither unreasonable nor unsupported by the evidence.

Finally, the ruling established a formidable sentencing precedent regarding dual corporate and personal penal multipliers. Even though the Provincial Court acquitted the appellants on Count 1 and convicted only on Count 2, it imposed a fine of $250,000 on Global Enviro Inc. and a separate fine of $250,000 on Ian George McIntyre personally. Because each fine represented approximately 77% of the $323,202.95 ITC claimed—the full claim being treated as the excess amount since the appellants conceded Global was not entitled to the credit—the combined penal sanction imposed on the corporation and its director equalled approximately 154% of the attempted tax credit refund, although the Court of Queen's Bench characterized each fine as being on the low end of the statutory range.
Comparative Summary Table of Legal Requirements, Taxpayer Failures, and Judicial Standards

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement implicated in R. v. Global Enviro Inc. and Ian George McIntyre and its companion Canadian SR&ED case law against the specific failures of the appellants and the governing standard of proof applied by Canadian courts.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Global Enviro
Judicial Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Requirement

cells: Temporal Cut-Off & Annual Expenditure Incurrence
ITA ss. 9, 37(1), 37(11), 127(9)

Filed Form T661 in January 2003 for the June 1, 2001 to May 31, 2002 taxation year, claiming an SR&ED ITC of $323,202.95 on $923,437 of contract expenditures for work largely performed before that period (the prototype was built in 1998).

Civil (TCC): Taxpayer must prove on a balance of probabilities via dated general ledgers, timesheets, and invoices that costs were incurred in the taxation year. Penal (ABPC/ABQB): Crown proved beyond a reasonable doubt, through the testimony of CRA auditors Dr. Patel and Ms. Quonn and documentary evidence (1998-dated photographs, the McIntyre and WHMIS invoices, and the April 3, 2003 letter), that after the March 24, 2003 audit meeting the accused misled the CRA about when the work was performed.

Entire ITC claim treated as unentitled (conceded by the appellants on appeal); acquittal on Count 1 under s. 239(1.1)(a), but conviction on Count 2 under s. 239(1.1)(e) for wilfully claiming an unentitled credit.
Corporate Attribution ("Performed By or On Behalf of the Taxpayer")

Claimed, as contract expenditures of the claim year, invoices dated May 31, 2002 from related parties (Ex-Cel, controlled by co-accused Page, and director McIntyre himself) and from WHMIS Inc. covering work performed before or outside the claim period.
Requires contemporaneous legal contracts, corporate minute books, and statements of work proving the claimant held technical direction and financial risk at the exact time the R&D was executed.
The courts did not adjudicate SR&ED entitlement, but the appellants conceded on appeal that Global Enviro Inc. was not entitled to the credit.
Prescribed Form Accuracy & Certification
ITA ss. 37(11), 239(1.1)(a), 239(1.1)(e); Form T661 E(01)

Form T661 E(01) (signed by J. R. Bateman) did not reflect when the work was performed; the trial judge found the appellants honestly believed it valid at filing, but after the audit meeting Mr. McIntyre provided misleading statements and documents to sustain the claim.

Under s. 239(1.1), the Crown must establish beyond a reasonable doubt both the falsity of the T661 statement (actus reus) and that the accused knew the statement was false or was wilfully blind (mens rea).
Acquittal on Count 1 (honest belief at the time of filing), but conviction on Count 2 for both the corporation and its director.
Technological Uncertainty & Advancement vs. Post-R&D Commercialization
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998); Zeuter Development Corp. v. The Queen (2006)

The courts did not assess technological uncertainty or advancement; the bitumen separation prototype had been built in 1998, before the claim period, yet the work was presented as performed during June 1, 2001 to May 31, 2002.

Contemporaneous technical documentation (hypotheses, test logs, analytical results) generated as the work progressed is required to separate eligible experimental development from routine engineering or commercial fabrication.

Where overstatement crosses from honest confusion (Zeuter) into knowingly misleading the CRA about when the work was performed (Global Enviro), the dispute escalates from civil disallowance to criminal prosecution.
Director & Officer Personal Penal Liability
ITA ss. 239(1.1)(g)–(h), 242; Criminal Code s. 686(1)(a)(iii)

Director Ian George McIntyre, after learning the CRA's claim-period requirement at the March 24, 2003 audit meeting, personally provided misleading explanations and documents (his own invoice, the WHMIS invoice and the April 3, 2003 letter) to pursue the claim.
Appellate court (2011 ABQB 32) reviews whether a properly instructed trier of fact could reasonably conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that the director acted wilfully.
Convictions and sentences upheld: $250,000 fine on Global Enviro Inc. (77% of ITC) and $250,000 fine on Ian George McIntyre personally (77% of ITC), totalling $500,000.

body.text: Applied Remedial Case Studies

To assist Canadian corporations, engineering leaders, and tax practitioners in navigating the exact legal and technical pitfalls exposed in R. v. Global Enviro Inc. and Ian George McIntyre, the following two applied industry case studies demonstrate step-by-step how high-risk projects must be structured, governed, documented, and claimed under the Income Tax Act (Canada).
Case Study 1: Multi-Year Industrial Waste Gasification Pilot (Overcoming Temporal Cut-Off, Fiscal Period Shifting, and Subcontractor Attribution Pitfalls)
Industry Scenario and Legal Vulnerability

Alberta Thermal Conversion Corp. ("ATCC"), a Calgary-based CCPC with a May 31 fiscal year-end, is developing a 275-tonne-per-day (275T) modular municipal solid waste gasification reactor. The project began in Fiscal Year 1 (June 1, 2024 – May 31, 2025) inside an unincorporated engineering syndicate led by ATCC's founder, before ATCC was formally incorporated on January 15, 2025. Furthermore, because ATCC experienced severe cash-flow constraints in Fiscal Year 1, external metallurgical testing contractors performed $400,000 of high-temperature refractory lining trials between February and May 2025, but agreed verbally to defer billing until ATCC closed its seed financing round in August 2025, which falls inside Fiscal Year 2 (June 1, 2025 – May 31, 2026). Additionally, ATCC missed the 18-month SR&ED filing deadline for a separate preliminary feasibility study conducted in a sister company during an earlier period. ATCC's Chief Financial Officer proposes bundling all 2024–2025 syndicate costs, the deferred contractor invoices, and the sister company's prior-period work into ATCC's Fiscal Year 2 Form T661 claim to maximize its 35% refundable CCPC Investment Tax Credit.

If executed as proposed, ATCC and its directors would replicate the exact violations prosecuted in Global Enviro (2009 ABPC 76; 2011 ABQB 32): claiming work completed in a prior reporting period, claiming work not legally performed "by or on behalf of" the corporate claimant during the active period, and—if the claim were then defended with misleading explanations or documents, as Global Enviro's was after its audit meeting—incurring liability under subsection 239(1.1) of the ITA.
Step 1: Project Governance and Fiscal Period Cut-Off Controls

To remediate these vulnerabilities, ATCC must first establish a formal SR&ED Tax Governance Charter overseen by an independent audit committee or external Canadian tax counsel prior to preparing Form T661. In accordance with sections 9 and 37(1) of the ITA, the governance protocol must enforce strict accrual cut-off segregation, mapping expenditures exclusively to the fiscal period in which the legal liability was incurred and the underlying technical work was physically performed. Specifically, the $400,000 of refractory trials physically performed between February and May 2025—subsequent to ATCC's January 15, 2025 incorporation—was legally incurred in Fiscal Year 1 (ending May 31, 2025), regardless of when the cash payment was remitted, subject only to the 180-day unpaid amount rules under subsection 78(4) of the ITA for accrued remuneration and subsection 127(26) of the ITA for other unpaid expenditures. Consequently, ATCC must file a dedicated Fiscal Year 1 Form T661 on or before November 30, 2026, which is the 18-month statutory deadline under subsection 37(11), to capture the February–May 2025 work legitimately, rather than shifting those activities into Fiscal Year 2.

Concurrently, ATCC's governance charter must mandate the permanent exclusion of all time-barred and pre-incorporation work. Any technical work performed prior to ATCC's January 15, 2025 incorporation by the unincorporated syndicate, as well as any time-barred work from the sister corporation's expired reporting periods, must be quarantined in a "Non-Claimable Historical Baseline" ledger. In the Fiscal Year 1 and Fiscal Year 2 Form T661 technical narratives (Part 2, Boxes 242 and 244), ATCC must explicitly disclose the pre-2025 work solely as prior art and baseline technology from which new, subsequent technological uncertainties arose, ensuring that zero historical costs contaminate the Part 3 and Part 4 financial schedules.
Step 2: Contractual Terms and Subcontractor Attribution Structuring

To satisfy the statutory requirement under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) that SR&ED be performed "on behalf of" ATCC, the corporation must overhaul its legal agreements with external contractors and related entities before work commences. Every third-party metallurgical lab and engineering subcontractor must execute a written Master Services Agreement (MSA) and Statement of Work (SOW) prior to initiating any experimental trials. Each SOW must explicitly stipulate that the work is performed in Canada exclusively on behalf of ATCC, that ATCC retains full technical direction, specifies the experimental parameters, and bears the financial risk of technological failure, that all foreground Intellectual Property (IP), raw test data, and failed prototype materials vest ab initio in ATCC, and that the contractor waives any independent right to claim SR&ED Investment Tax Credits in respect of the contracted activities.

Furthermore, contractors must be contractually obligated to issue monthly progress invoices tied to verifiable technical milestones. These invoices must detail the exact dates of work performance, the names and hourly logs of Canadian personnel, specific test rig identifiers, and a clear financial separation between eligible experimental testing—which is 80% eligible for ITCs under subsection 127(9)—and ineligible commercial equipment fabrication or capital expenditures.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Experimentation Tracking

To prove that genuine SR&ED occurred within each distinct fiscal period, ATCC must implement a digital Project Lifecycle Management (PLM) and version-control engineering repository equipped with immutable cryptographic timestamps. On May 31 of each fiscal year, the Vice President of Engineering must generate a frozen "Fiscal Year-End Technical Snapshot" archiving all CAD models, mass-and-energy balance simulations, thermocouple log files, and syngas chromatography results generated up to 11:59 PM on May 31.

Where a complex technological uncertainty—such as preventing tar condensation and vitrification bridging in the 275T gasification throat at 1,200°C—spans both Fiscal Year 1 and Fiscal Year 2, the Form T661 narrative for each year must isolate the exact hypotheses formulated and tested within those specific 12 months. Fiscal Year 1 documentation will record Hypotheses 1.1 through 1.4 concerning thermal-shock refractory spalling tests, while Fiscal Year 2 documentation will record Hypotheses 2.1 through 2.6 concerning modified secondary oxygen-injection nozzle geometries, thereby preventing any audit allegation of retroactive narrative recycling.
Case Study 2: Cleantech Flue-Gas Scrubbing and Syngas Refining System (Overcoming Technological Uncertainty, Commercial-vs-Experimental Blurring, and Form T661 Disclosure Pitfalls)
Industry Scenario and Legal Vulnerability

Prairie CleanAir Systems Inc. ("PCAS"), an Edmonton-based environmental engineering company, previously claimed and received SR&ED tax credits between 2022 and 2024 for developing a novel catalytic Venturi scrubber that removes hydrogen sulfide (H₂S) and siloxanes from municipal waste syngas. By late 2024, the core catalytic formulation and fluid-dynamic geometry were successfully validated, and in 2025 PCAS began manufacturing and installing three full-scale commercial units (550T capacity) for municipal clients in Alberta. During the 2025 commercial installations, PCAS engineers encountered site-specific pressure drops and mechanical vibration issues requiring 4,500 hours of field adjustments, programmable logic controller (PLC) tuning, and heat-exchanger re-piping. PCAS's President and sole director, facing working capital pressures and relying on the fact that the CRA approved their 2022–2024 claims without audit, instructs an external contingency-fee preparer to file a 2025 Form T661 claiming the entire $1.8 million commercial fabrication and field commissioning budget as an ongoing "experimental prototype scale-up," backdating internal test protocols to make routine field commissioning appear as structured scientific experimentation.

This scenario combines the exact traps of Zeuter Development—continuing to claim a project after technological uncertainties have been resolved and routine commercial deployment has begun—and Global Enviro and Les éléments chauffants Tempora—knowingly misrepresenting when, or what, work was performed in order to sustain a claim, and exposing both the corporation and the signing director to criminal prosecution and 50%–200% penal fines under subsection 239(1.1) of the ITA.
Step 1: Technical Triage Using the Five-Question Northwest Hydraulic Standard

Before any tax schedule is drafted, PCAS's engineering and legal teams must conduct a formal "SR&ED Eligibility Gate Review" applying the five criteria from Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen to decouple routine commercial engineering from genuine new experimental development. Standard PLC tuning, mechanical vibration dampening using off-the-shelf isolation mounts, and re-piping heat exchangers to match site layouts are resolved via standard mechanical and chemical engineering practice. Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, which explicitly excludes routine engineering, commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, and style or site adaptations, these 2025 commissioning costs must be completely excluded from the SR&ED claim.

Conversely, suppose that during the 550T scale-up, PCAS discovers that scaling the Venturi throat diameter beyond 400 mm induces non-linear acoustic cavitation that destroys the wash-coat catalyst within 72 hours—a phenomenon that cannot be predicted by existing multiphase computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models or standard chemical engineering principles. PCAS must carve out only the specific systematic investigation undertaken to resolve this non-linear acoustic cavitation phenomenon as a discrete, narrowly scoped SR&ED project.
Step 2: Commercial Contract Restructuring and Funded Research Compliance

Because the acoustic cavitation problem emerged during the execution of commercial municipal supply contracts, PCAS must address both the commercial asset versus experimental prototype rules and the contract payment reduction rules under subsections 127(9), 127(11.1), and 127(18) to (20) of the ITA. Under the CRA's administrative policies on Experimental Production and Commercial Assets Having Incremental SR&ED, the $1.8 million cost of fabricating the commercial 550T municipal plant is ineligible capital or cost-of-goods-sold. However, if PCAS constructs a temporary, instrumented slip-stream bypass test module at its Edmonton facility specifically to test five experimental acoustic-baffle catalyst geometries, and scraps the test cartridges upon completion, the materials consumed or transformed in that slip-stream loop—along with the direct engineering hours spent designing and analyzing those trials—qualify as eligible SR&ED expenditures under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) and subsection 127(9).

To prevent the municipal client's purchase payments from being characterized as a "contract payment" (as defined in subsection 127(9)) that reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures dollar-for-dollar under subsection 127(18), PCAS's commercial supply contract must clearly specify a fixed price for delivering the commercial unit meeting standard specifications, while PCAS's internal slip-stream R&D project is chartered, funded, and owned 100% internally by PCAS at its sole financial risk.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Experimentation Tracking and General Ledger Segregation

To eliminate any risk of administrative penalties under subsection 163(2) or penal charges under subsection 239(1.1) for overstating claims, PCAS must enforce strict financial and technical record-keeping pursuant to subsection 230(1) of the ITA. Engineers must record their time daily in an electronic time-tracking system using distinct work-breakdown-structure (WBS) codes that segregate WBS-100 (Commercial Fabrication & Field Commissioning - Ineligible) from WBS-900 (Acoustic Cavitation Catalyst SR&ED Hypothesis Testing - Eligible). Every WBS-900 entry must cross-reference a specific experiment identifier in the laboratory notebook. Furthermore, external SR&ED consultants must be contractually barred from creating or backdating test protocols; instead, the Form T661 Part 2 technical narrative must be synthesized directly from contemporaneous test logs, failed catalyst scanning electron microscopy (SEM-EDS) micrographs, and CFD divergence reports generated during the 2025 fiscal year.
Step 4: Director Sign-Off and Verification Protocol

To protect PCAS's director from the personal conviction and $250,000 fine suffered by Ian George McIntyre in Global Enviro, PCAS must implement a two-stage "Director Due Diligence Sign-Off" prior to executing Form T661. First, the Lead Professional Engineer (P.Eng.) who directly supervised the 2025 slip-stream trials must sign an internal representation letter confirming that every statement in the Form T661 technical narrative accurately reflects experiments physically conducted between the start and end dates of the 2025 taxation year. Second, the corporate Controller must provide the director with a line-by-line reconciliation proving that all claimed T4 wages, materials consumed, and contractor invoices match the audited 2025 financial statements and exclude all prior-period (2022–2024) costs and commercial plant fabrication expenses.
Summary of Remedial Controls Across Both Case Studies
The table below synthesizes the operational and documentary controls required to neutralize the legal risks identified in R. v. Global Enviro Inc. and Ian George McIntyre.

body.text: Strategic Conclusions and Advisory Recommendations for Canadian SR&ED Practitioners

The decisions of the Provincial Court of Alberta (2009 ABPC 76) and the Court of Queen's Bench of Alberta (2011 ABQB 32) in R. v. Global Enviro Inc. and Ian George McIntyre stand as an enduring warning to Canadian corporate claimants, company directors, and SR&ED advisors. While the SR&ED program under sections 37 and 127 of the Income Tax Act remains one of the federal government's premier fiscal incentives for industrial innovation, Global Enviro demonstrates that the Canada Revenue Agency and the Public Prosecution Service of Canada will not hesitate to bypass civil reassessment procedures and invoke the criminal machinery of subsection 239(1.1) when a taxpayer, after being told of the governing requirements, misleads CRA auditors about project timelines or the work performed in order to sustain an SR&ED claim.

Three overarching legal principles emerge from this jurisprudence for Canadian tax practitioners. First, temporal integrity is as critical as substantive technical eligibility: even where development work occurred in an earlier period, such as the pre-June 2001 work on Global Enviro Inc.'s bitumen separation prototype (built in 1998), claiming prior-period work in a later taxation year, as occurred in the January 2003 filing, invalidates the claim, and knowingly misleading the CRA to sustain such a claim—as the appellants did after the March 24, 2003 audit meeting—constitutes an offence under subsection 239(1.1) of the ITA. The 18-month filing deadline under subsection 37(11) operates as an absolute statutory bar that cannot be circumvented by re-dating work on Form T661.

Second, the corporate veil offers no shield to signing directors. By affirming a separate $250,000 fine against Global Enviro Inc. and a personal $250,000 fine against director Ian George McIntyre—each representing 77% of the ITC claimed, for a combined penal sanction of 154% of the claim—the Alberta courts established that corporate directors bear personal penal responsibility for the veracity of Form T661 disclosures. Subsequent Canadian decisions, notably R. v. Les éléments chauffants Tempora inc. (2017 QCCQ 2684) and R. v. Avard (2014 QCCQ 9716), have explicitly relied on Global Enviro in imposing massive fines and criminal convictions for fraudulent SR&ED claims.

Finally, contemporaneous governance is the only viable defence against both civil disallowance and penal liability. To remain safely on the civil side of Canadian tax administration—and to satisfy the stringent evidentiary threshold of Northwest Hydraulic—Canadian taxpayers must embed real-time fiscal period cut-off controls, explicit pre-performance contractor agreements, segregated WBS time-tracking, and rigorous pre-filing verification protocols into their routine engineering and accounting workflows.
